key_insight: A 127-qubit IBM Eagle processor can run an end-to-end 10-class MNIST quantum classifier, but the practical gain is workflow efficiency rather than higher accuracy.
engineering_relevance: The paper shows a deployable NISQ pipeline that shifts training off hardware, uses hardware only for inference, and scales throughput with quantum multi-programming.
method: Two-phase training: classical gradient-based optimization for the encoder/readout, then gradient-free optimization for quantum parameters.
Quantum multi-programming packs multiple trained circuit copies onto one device for parallel inference.
A controlled fine-tuning study compares on-hardware training versus simulator-trained deployment.
evidence_signal: The system was evaluated on 10-class MNIST and benchmarked against a matched-capacity classical network, with no measurable accuracy gain from on-hardware fine-tuning and no mean-accuracy cost from multi-programmed inference.
watch_item: The approach does not show a per-parameter accuracy advantage over a comparable classical model, so its value depends on hardware access, job submission limits, and NISQ noise conditions.
paper_title: Image Classification on IBM Quantum Computers
